text: For six months in 1893, Jackson Park was not a park.
The World's Columbian Exposition was built to mark four hundred years since Columbus reached the Americas.
The dedication ceremonies were held in October of 1892, near the four-hundredth anniversary, but the gates did not open to the public until the first of May the next year.
The grounds covered about six hundred and eighty-six acres of lakefront that had been mostly marsh and sand.
The whole thing cost more than twenty-eight million dollars.
And almost none of it was meant to last.
On opening day, President Grover Cleveland stood on a platform at the head of the Court of Honor.
A little after noon he pressed a golden telegraph key, and the signal started the great steam engine over in Machinery Hall.
Flags dropped, fountains rose, and a choir broke into the Hallelujah chorus.
About two hundred thousand people were there to see it.
A week after the gates opened, the Panic of 1893 reached Chicago, a financial collapse that became the worst depression the country had seen.
By that winter, with the fair's work gone, something like a hundred thousand men were out of work on Chicago's streets.
The White City sold a dream of order at the exact moment the economy outside it was falling apart.
